title: Gifts and fruits (CCC 1830–1832)
hook: seven gifts of the Spirit, twelve fruits

segments.voice: Yesterday, virtue: a firm habit of doing good, built one act at a time. Your line was habits of good. Was your small good act any easier the second time? Day one thousand one hundred seventeen.

"There shall come forth a rod out of the root of Jesse, and a flower shall rise up out of his root." That's Isaiah, in the Douay-Rheims. An old root in the ground, and out of it, something green and new. On that shoot, Isaiah says, the spirit of the Lord will rest, and he names what that spirit brings, one after another. Christians have read the passage as being about Jesus, the son of David, born of Jesse's line. And the Catechism takes Isaiah's list and says it doesn't stop with him. Today: the gifts, and what grows from them.
screen: `AN OLD ROOT.` → `A SHOOT FROM THE ROOT OF JESSE.` → `THE SPIRIT RESTS ON HIM.`

segments.voice: Yesterday was about virtues built by effort. The Catechism says that isn't the whole picture. The moral life, it says, is also held up by the gifts of the Holy Spirit: lasting dispositions that make a person docile, ready to follow the Spirit's promptings. It lists seven gifts: wisdom, understanding, counsel, fortitude, knowledge, piety, and fear of the Lord. They belong in their fullness to Christ, son of David, it says, and they finish and perfect the virtues of those who receive them. Fortitude is courage that holds. Counsel is knowing what to do in a tangle. Fear of the Lord, as some teachers explain it, isn't terror but awe, the kind that keeps God God. So that's the root. Then the fruit. The Catechism says the fruits of the Spirit are perfections that the Spirit forms in a person, as the first fruits of eternal glory, and that the Church's tradition lists twelve. They come from Paul's letter to the Galatians. In the Douay-Rheims: "But the fruit of the Spirit is, charity, joy, peace, patience, benignity, goodness, longanimity, mildness, faith, modesty, continency, chastity." Some of those old words need unpacking. Benignity is kindness. Longanimity is a long, patient endurance, a slow fuse. Continency is self-control. Here's what ties it together. A gift is something received, hidden, like a root. A fruit is what shows on the branch, where other people can see it and be fed by it. Nobody tastes your fortitude. They taste your patience on a hard afternoon. So in this teaching, the gifts are given, and the fruits are how anyone can tell.
screen: `THE GIFTS: READY FOR THE SPIRIT.` · `SEVEN GIFTS, FULL IN CHRIST.` · `TWELVE FRUITS, FROM GALATIANS.` · `THE ROOT IS HIDDEN, THE FRUIT FEEDS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look for one fruit today. Settle, and breathe. Go back over the last day or two, slowly. Look for one moment, in you or in someone near you, where one of those fruits showed up. A bit of patience at a checkout line. Gentleness with a tired child. Joy that came from nowhere. Peace in a tense meeting. Don't hunt for something grand. Find one, and stay with it. Who was fed by it? If you pray, you can give thanks for it. If you don't, just let it be noticed. The bell holds the time.
Gifts and fruits. The gifts of the Spirit, wisdom through fear of the Lord, make a person ready to follow God; the fruits, charity through chastity, are what grows and shows. Today's word.
Your line: gifts become fruit. Today, watch for one of the fruits in someone else, and tell them you saw it. Day one thousand one hundred seventeen.

howItsDone: Catholics associate the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit with baptism and confirmation, where the bishop prays for them, and some learn the gifts and the twelve fruits by heart before confirmation.

what it means: the gifts make a person ready for the Spirit, and the fruits are what that readiness grows into, where others can see it.
what a scholar hears: Isaiah 11 read of Christ, son of David, gifts that perfect the virtues, and a tradition counting twelve fruits from Galatians 5.

notes: CCC 1830–1832 paraphrased (copyrighted translation): gifts as permanent dispositions making one docile (1830), the seven gifts, full in Christ son of David, completing the virtues (1831), fruits as perfections, first fruits of eternal glory, tradition lists twelve (1832). The counts seven and twelve come from these paragraphs.
Please verify the exact Douay-Rheims (Challoner) wording of Isaiah 11:1 and Galatians 5:22–23 before release.
Glosses of benignity, longanimity, continency, fortitude, counsel and fear of the Lord are plain-language explanations, not Catechism quotations; confirm.
The Greek of Galatians 5 lists fewer fruits than the Vulgate; deliberately not stated (claims rule). Keeper may wish to add.
howItsDone's confirmation prayer for the seven gifts is general Catholic practice; confirm.
